claims.text: Near-equimolar HfNbTaTiZr is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The target HfNbTaTiZr samples contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A machine-learning interatomic potential can robustly separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Training on multi-temperature phonon and electron scattering data is sufficient to enable separation of the two heat-transport channels.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by 25–40% relative to previous defect-free or Debye-based methods.
The model will integrate ab initio calculations containing controlled defect configurations with measured thermal-conductivity data at multiple temperatures and oxygen concentrations.
Oxygen impurities induce local atomic distortions and additional scattering pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-induced distortions and scattering pathways influence both phonon and electronic transport.
Learning real defect-induced scattering will allow the model to isolate phonon and electron conduction more accurately than a single-parameter Debye approach.
Learning real defect-induced scattering will outperform defect-free DFT simulations.
Previous first-principles or phenomenological models cannot fully account for the multiple principal elements, oxygen scattering, and complex atomic environment of HfNbTaTiZr.
Across 200–600 K, the model's total-conductivity predictions will be 25–40% closer to experiment than prior predictions.
The model will maintain strong predictive accuracy below 200 K and up to 1200 K.
The approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr over 100–1200 K and oxygen concentrations up to approximately 1 wt.%.
Predictions outside 100–1200 K, above approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, or for substantially different alloy compositions are uncertain without additional validation.
Electrical resistivity and Seebeck-coefficient measurements can provide separate experimental lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions for the proposed comparison.
Deviation of the predicted lattice and electronic contributions by more than approximately 25–40% across multiple temperature–oxygen points would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central improvement is defined as 25–40% better accuracy relative to previous methods, but the falsification rule instead uses 25–40% absolute deviation from experiment and does not require comparison with the prior methods. Thus the stated test does not decisively test the claimed relative improvement.
